description: Bridge march guide: hold a glute bridge and lift one foot at a time to build glutes and deep core control, with mistakes and easier or harder versions.
intro: The bridge march starts as a regular bridge, then you lift one foot and the other while your hips stay up. Each lift shifts the load to one side, so your glutes and deep core must stop the pelvis from dropping or twisting. It builds the stable base the pelvis needs for walking, lifting and training.
feel: You should feel both glutes working, with extra effort in the standing leg each time a foot lifts. Your belly feels gently braced and your hips stay high and level. Watch for breath holding, an arched lower back or pushing down into the pelvis. If your hips sink or rock with each step, make the march smaller.

mistakes.right: Raise the foot an inch or two at first. The goal is a steady pelvis, not a big leg movement.

mistakes.wrong: Holding your breath through the set
mistakes.right: Breathe out as each foot lifts and in as it comes down. Keep the rhythm slow.
If your hips drop, lower down, rest and restart with fewer marches.

easier: Lift only the heel, keeping the toes down, or rest after every two marches.
harder: Pause with one foot up for 2 to 3 seconds, straighten the lifted leg, or slow each march.
who: Lifters and anyone working on core and hip control, especially once a plain bridge feels easy.
skip: Scale back or skip with back pain during bridges, hip pain, a hernia or recent abdominal surgery. If you notice bulging along the middle of your belly, pelvic heaviness or leaking during the move, get checked by a physiotherapist. Stop if it hurts.

faq.q: What does the bridge march work?
faq.a: The glutes and hamstrings, plus the deep core muscles that keep the pelvis level, one side at a time.

faq.q: Should my hips stay perfectly still?
faq.a: Aim for as little movement as you can manage. A small wobble is normal at first, but a big drop means it is too hard for now.
